note: The traditional New Year's Eve food in northern China, usually made together by the whole family.

gloss: (slang) service provider for Shadowsocks or similar software for circumventing Internet censorship
note: Online slang for a paid proxy service used to get past the Great Firewall. 换机场 means switching providers, not airports.
Rural China as opposed to the cities, tied to rural household registration. Saying someone grew up in 农村 suggests poorer schools and fewer chances.
Also the polite way to address a student whose name is unknown: 这位同学. Old classmates often still do each other favours decades later.
At New Year, 走亲戚 means making the rounds of relatives, who often ask about pay and marriage plans.

gloss: form of address used by children for a male one generation older
note: Children call any man of their parents' generation 叔叔, from a friend's dad to the security guard. No family tie is needed.

gloss: term of address for a woman of one's mother's generation
note: Used to address shop assistants, neighbours and a friend's mother alike. Polite and a little familial.
Families address a hired nanny or childminder as 阿姨 ("auntie"), a polite, family-style term for what is paid work.
Traditionally seen as marrying into her husband's family. 婆媳矛盾, friction between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, is a stock theme of family dramas.
A husband's everyday word for his wife, common in the north. Affectionate and down to earth, like "the missus".
A gentle way to speak of a death, as in 他走了 ("he's gone"), avoiding the blunt 死.
In political language: 红歌 (red songs), 红色旅游 (red tourism) and 红色经典 celebrate the Party and the revolution.
Applied to a person only as an insult: 你真不是东西 ("you're scum") treats someone as a thing.
Mostly in the modest phrase 一点小意思 ("just a little something") when giving a gift. 意思意思 can hint that a tip or payment is expected.
Connections built on favours owed and returned. A job found 靠关系 came through someone calling in a favour.
Can be an easy-going shrug or a criticism of sloppiness. 差不多先生, Mr About-Right, is a famous satire of people who never get things exactly right.
From a host, 随便 is generous. As an answer to 吃什么？ ("what shall we eat?") it is a famous source of trouble between couples.

gloss: to go to a lot of trouble
note: Mostly heard as 辛苦了, said to a courier, a colleague or a host to thank them for their effort.

gloss: to bother sb; to put sb to trouble
note: 麻烦你 before a request works like "sorry to trouble you" and softens it: 麻烦你帮我拿一下 ("could you grab that for me?").
Polite by holding back. 别客气 means drop the ceremony, since being too 客气 with someone close keeps them at a distance.
Strongly positive: crowds, noise and activity make a place or festival feel happy. 看热闹 means watching a commotion as a bystander.
Being blamed or mistreated unfairly and having to swallow it. A common apology or comfort: 让你受委屈了, "sorry you had to put up with that".
Love shown as concern: parents 心疼 a child who works too hard or gets hurt. Affectionate, not pity.
Said about money or things lost or wasted: 新手机摔坏了，真心疼 ("my new phone cracked, it really hurts").
Said of people and things alike: 舍不得走 ("hate to leave"), 舍不得扔 ("can't bring myself to throw it out").
Said lightly when squeezing past someone or asking a favour, half apology and half embarrassment.

gloss: section of society operating independently of mainstream society, out of reach of the law; the milieu in which wuxia tales play out (cf. 武俠|武侠[wu3 xia2])
note: The world of wandering swordsmen in wuxia stories, ruled by reputation and loyalty. Now also any world outside official rules: 人在江湖，身不由己.
Standing in other people's eyes. Paying the bill gives a friend 面子; contradicting a boss in public makes him lose it.
A favour that creates a debt. Accepting help means owing a 人情 (欠人情), which is expected to be repaid, sometimes years later.

gloss: a connection (sb with whom one has dealings on the basis of "scratch my back and I'll scratch yours")
note: Said disapprovingly, usually behind someone's back, about a hire or student who got in through connections.

gloss: (fig.) to pull strings; to use connections
note: Literally "go through the back door". Usually disapproving: a dinner, a gift or a word with someone in charge to get a hospital bed or a school place.

gloss: devoted to one's parents (and grandparents etc)
note: Seen as a moral duty more than a feeling: supporting parents in old age, deferring to their wishes and, for many families, giving them grandchildren.

gloss: fate or chance that brings people together
note: Said when people meet by chance or click at once: 真有缘分 ("it must be fate"). 没缘分 is a common way to say a relationship wasn't meant to be.
Central to traditional medicine and martial arts, where illness is often explained as 气 that is blocked or out of balance.

gloss: to suffer from excessive internal heat (TCM)
note: An everyday diagnosis: spicy food, late nights or stress are blamed for sore throats and mouth ulcers, and the usual cure is herbal tea.
Building up the body with nourishing food or tonics. After an illness, chicken soup is a classic way to 补身体.
Tied to where a family is officially registered. It decides which school a child can attend and whether a city treats someone as a full local.

gloss: work unit (place of employment, esp. in the PRC prior to economic reform)
note: Before the reforms, the 单位 also gave out housing and medical care and approved marriages. People still say 我们单位 for their workplace.
A secure job, usually in the state sector. Many parents still prefer one for their children over better-paid private work.

gloss: (fig.) to take the plunge (e.g. leave a secure job, or enter prostitution etc)
note: Best known for quitting a secure state job to go into business, as many officials and teachers did in the 1980s and 90s. Can also mean entering the sex trade.

gloss: (of a worker) be to laid off
note: Linked above all to the 1990s restructuring of state enterprises, when millions of workers lost jobs once thought to be for life.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2017) (of a society) to become more and more of a rat race; to become increasingly competitive (due to limited resources)
note: Competition where everyone works harder and nobody gets ahead, as when a whole class starts studying at 5 a.m. because others do.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2021) to opt out of the rat race
note: Online slang for opting out: a modest life instead of wearing oneself out for a promotion. Often set against 内卷.

gloss: (fig.) to loaf on the job; to be slack; to take it easy
note: Office slang, often self-mocking: 上班摸鱼 means scrolling a phone or chatting when there's work to do.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2017) (coll.) chill about everything (typically used to describe young people who don't buy into aspirational society)
note: Online slang for young people who stop competing and accept whatever comes. Often self-mocking: 佛系青年.
Treated as a virtue: 能吃苦 ("able to take hardship") is praise for a child or a worker, and 吃苦耐劳 is a stock compliment.
Ordinary people in contrast to officials and those in power. Common in both casual talk and official speeches.
Used for the educated as a social class expected to serve the nation. The word has a long history, from honoured scholars to targets of political campaigns.
Anyone holding a post in the Party or state system, from a village official up. At school, class monitors are 班干部.
A word of political language: the people the Party says it serves. Officials are told to 深入群众, "go among the masses".
The old revolutionary address between equals. Now it sounds official or nostalgic, and it is also a word gay people use for themselves.
Official language and textbooks use it with heroic, positive weight, above all for the Communist revolution.

gloss: reform and opening up (Chinese policy introduced in 1978)
note: Often used as a dividing line in life stories: 改革开放以前 means the poorer, closed China before the boom.

gloss: educated youth (esp. those sent to work in rural areas during the Cultural Revolution) (abbr. for 知識青年|知识青年[zhi1 shi5 qing1 nian2])
note: Millions lost years of schooling this way, and many still tell stories of their villages. The movement was called 上山下乡.

gloss: forced agricultural experience for city intellectuals
note: The campaign that sent city teenagers to labour on remote farms in the 1960s and 70s. Many stayed for a decade.

gloss: migrant worker (who moved from a rural area of China to a city to find work)
note: Rural people working on city building sites and in factories, usually without city household registration. Many leave children behind in the village.

gloss: to work a temporary or casual job
note: Working for a boss, often casual or migrant work. 出去打工 means leaving the countryside for city jobs; students' part-time jobs are also 打工.
An ironic self-label used online by office workers joking about grinding away for a boss: 早安，打工人 ("morning, fellow wage slaves").

gloss: (increased) passenger transportation around Chinese New Year
note: Means packed trains, long journeys standing up and tickets that sell out within seconds, as people head home for New Year.

gloss: money wrapped in red as a gift
note: Cash in a red envelope, given at New Year, weddings and birthdays. The amount is expected to suit the occasion and the relationship.
A cash bribe, typically to a doctor or official in return for better treatment.

gloss: to celebrate the Chinese New Year
note: Means going home for the family dinner, red envelopes and fireworks. 回家过年 is the reason for the yearly travel rush.

gloss: Pure Brightness Festival or Tomb Sweeping Day (in early April)
note: As a festival, the day families visit graves, tidy them and burn paper offerings. It is also one of the 24 solar terms, in early April.
Ancestors as a family line owed respect, honoured at graves and tablets. 丢祖宗的脸 ("shame your ancestors") is a serious rebuke.
The word of school songs and National Day speeches, said with pride and a sense of duty.
Not necessarily where someone grew up. A person raised in Shanghai may still call a village visited once a year their 老家.
Longing for one's hometown, a common theme in poetry and emigrant writing. The moon is its classic image.

gloss: in old age, an expatriate returns home
note: Literally "fallen leaves return to the roots". Said of emigrants or people far from home who want to return, or be buried, in their home town.
A Confucian duty to honour, obey and care for parents, not just affection. 孝顺 ("dutiful to parents") is high praise for a son or daughter.
The Confucian order of correct behaviour: who pours tea for whom, who sits where, how respect is shown. 礼貌 ("manners") comes from it.
The central Confucian virtue, kindness grounded in human relationships. 仁者爱人: "the humane person loves others."
A core Confucian virtue: doing what is right even at a cost. In old novels, it is the loyalty of sworn brothers who would die for each other.
In Daoism, the natural order behind all things, which can't be fully named, only followed. The 道德经 opens 道可道，非常道.
The Confucian ideal, the opposite of 小人. Common in sayings like 君子动口不动手 ("a gentleman argues with words, not fists").
Someone who schemes against others behind their back. A strong insult; 防小人 means watching out for backstabbers.
In classical texts, the whole world seen as one realm under a ruler, with China at its centre. Still common in sayings like 天下无敌 ("unbeatable anywhere").
A grand, historical word for a country as something won and held. 打江山 means fighting to win the country; 坐江山 means ruling it.
In China it covers both the 56 official ethnic groups and the single 中华民族, the Chinese nation.
Taught as a core duty from school onward and common in official slogans, so it can sound heartfelt or simply expected.

gloss: respectful form of address for older men
note: Used for taxi drivers, plumbers, cooks and other skilled workers: 师傅，去火车站 ("to the train station, please").
Also a flattering way to address customers: street vendors call out 老板，来看看 ("boss, come take a look").
Being 讲究 about food means caring about season, region and presentation. It reads as refinement, not fussiness; 有讲究 means there's a proper way to do it.
Making do with something less than ideal. 将就一下 ("it'll do for now") is a common way to accept a small flat or a plain meal.
A common answer to 最近怎么样？: 凑合 ("getting by"), meaning not great, not terrible. 凑合着用 means making do with something.

gloss: to repeat sth over and over again
note: Usually a complaint about pointless effort: 别瞎折腾了 ("stop messing about"). Moving house three times in a year is 折腾.
Often unpaid and expected. In tech it is tied to 996: 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.
Used for any superior, even a middle manager, and as a form of address to their face. 领导说了算 ("the boss decides") is office talk.
Slang for a sex worker. As a result, calling a waitress 小姐 can sound insulting on the mainland, so people say 服务员 or 美女 instead.
Also a casual way to address any young woman, used by shop assistants and waiters. Friendly, not flirtatious.
Used by vendors and shop staff to address any young man, whatever his looks. 美女 is the female equivalent.
An older, reverent title for a teacher or great scholar: Lu Xun is still called 鲁迅先生.

gloss: fellow townsman; fellow villager; sb from the same hometown
note: Meeting a 老乡 far from home creates an instant bond, often with a switch to dialect. Also a friendly way to address rural people.
Casual, between men: 好哥们 is a close friend. Also used to address a stranger, like "mate" or "bro".
A common informal word women use for their best friend: 我闺蜜. Originally short for 闺中密友.
Usually a partner with marriage in view. 有对象了吗？("Seeing anyone?") is a standard question from relatives at New Year.

gloss: arranged interview to evaluate a proposed marriage partner (Taiwan pr. [xiang4 qin1])
note: Often set up by an aunt or parents. Job, flat and family background come up early.

gloss: (coll.) "leftover woman" – a woman who remains single beyond the typical marrying age
note: A dismissive label for a woman still single in her late twenties. Now often used critically or ironically.
Paid by the groom's family to the bride's. In some regions the sum is very large, and disputes over it can end an engagement.
A wife's word for her husband's mother; his father is 公公. Tension between 婆媳 (mother-in-law and daughter-in-law) is a staple of TV drama.
Said from the husband's side; the person a groom must win over. Jokes say a man needs a flat and a car before the 丈母娘 will approve.

gloss: (of a prospective marriage partner) an appropriate match
note: Still applied to real matches: parents weigh jobs, wealth and family background, and a mismatch can end a relationship.

gloss: to carry on one's ancestral line
note: Traditionally means having a son to carry on the surname. Older relatives still bring it up when pushing for a grandson.

gloss: (of parents) to bring up children for the purpose of being looked after in old age
note: The traditional expectation that children, especially sons, will support their parents in old age in place of a pension.

gloss: to bring honor to one's ancestors
note: Success in exams or business counts as an honour for the whole family line, not just the individual.

gloss: lit. to hope one's son becomes a dragon (idiom); fig. to long for one' s child to succeed in life
note: Used of parents who push their children hard, spending heavily on tutoring and classes. Often paired with 望女成凤 for daughters.

gloss: college entrance exam (especially as abbr. for 普通高等學校招生全國統一考試|普通高等学校招生全国统一考试[Pu3 tong1 Gao1 deng3 Xue2 xiao4 Zhao1 sheng1 Quan2 guo2 Tong3 yi1 Kao3 shi4])
note: Held each June, it largely decides which university a student enters. Streets near exam halls are kept quiet while it runs.

gloss: top scorer in college entrance examination 高考[gao1 kao3]
note: Popular name for each province's top 高考 scorer, though officials now discourage publicising them. The title comes from the old imperial exam champion.

gloss: to sit an entrance exam for a graduate program
note: Usually means a year of library mornings and flashcards, competing with millions of other candidates in one national exam.

gloss: sb who has come back to China after gaining overseas experience (a pun on 海龜|海龟[hai3 gui1])
note: Once a mark of prized talent. A foreign degree is now less of a golden ticket in the job market.
Student and online slang, usually admiring. The opposite is 学渣, a student who does badly.

gloss: (neologism, c. 2020) to arrange an intensive schedule of activities for one's child to maximize achievement
note: From 打鸡血 ("inject chicken blood"), slang for being pumped up. Often used critically for parents who fill a child's week with Olympiad maths, piano and English.
Many children spend evenings and weekends in them to gain a few more exam points.
Officially ranked top tier. A 重点 high school feeds the best universities, and parents move house to get a child in.

gloss: (of an education system) to be exam-oriented
note: Mostly heard in 应试教育, a complaint about rote learning aimed only at passing exams.
Often used to judge public manners: 没素质 is a sharp criticism of someone who litters or jumps queues.
Usually the state system and its jobs. 体制内 ("inside the system") means a government or state job, valued for stability; 体制外 is everything else.

gloss: authorized staffing allocation in government or public institutions (excluding temporary or contract staff)
note: A permanent official post, valued for its security. Young people take exam after exam to 考编 ("get a post").
People sigh 这就是命 ("that's fate") when hardship seems unavoidable, half acceptance, half complaint. 认命 means to accept one's lot.
Pasted on doors at New Year, often upside down: 倒 ("upside down") sounds like 到 ("arrived"), so 福倒了 means fortune has arrived.
Said of people blessed with a good life, like grandparents surrounded by grandchildren: 你真有福气 ("you're so lucky").
Said with satisfaction when a wrongdoer gets what's coming: 这就是报应. Also a warning: 会有报应的 ("you'll pay for this").
Also used loosely for things that come round again: 时尚是个轮回 ("fashion goes in cycles").

gloss: to devote oneself to spiritual development (esp. Buddhism or Daoism)
note: Also used loosely for disciplined, patient living. 修行在个人 ("the practice is up to each person") is said of any skill a teacher can only begin.
In Buddhist belief, merit earned through good deeds. Donating to a temple or releasing captive fish (放生) adds 功德.
Praise for upright integrity that won't bend to power, often said of scholars and writers. A literary, admiring word.
High praise in history and literature, for officials and scholars who refused to serve an invader even at the cost of their lives.
Used as praise for refusing to bow or beg: a poor man who won't take charity on humiliating terms has 骨气.
Moral praise, common in official language and martial arts stories. 一身正气 describes someone upright who stands up against wrongdoing.
The code of loyalty between friends, especially sworn brothers who stand by each other even against the law. 讲义气 is high praise.
Loyalty between friends, the code of brotherhood and martial-arts stories. A friend who 讲义气 lends money without asking why.
Mostly in phrases about favours: 看在老同学的情面上 ("for old times' sake"); 不讲情面 means treating friends no differently from strangers.
Polite talk not meant literally, like compliments at dinner. 不用客套 means "no need to stand on ceremony".
Mostly business entertaining: banquets and drinking with clients or officials. Often a complaint: 今晚又有应酬 ("another work dinner tonight").

gloss: to toast; to propose a toast
note: Common at banquets, especially toward seniors: stand, hold the glass lower than theirs, and drink, often round after round.
Literally "dry the cup": the glass is meant to be emptied, not sipped.
Means paying, not just inviting: 今天我请客 ("it's on me"). Friends often argue at the till over who gets to pay.

gloss: to pay the bill; to pick up the tab
note: Also means taking responsibility or paying the price: 谁为这次失败买单？("who pays for this failure?").
In business people are judged by their 人脉 as much as by their skills. 人脉广 means well connected.
Often closed and hard to enter; getting into a new 圈子 takes introductions, banquets and favours. 圈内人 means an insider.
Casual and self-mocking: 你混得怎么样？ ("how are you getting on?"). 混日子 means just getting by without effort.
The saying 吃亏是福 ("losing out is a blessing") teaches accepting small losses. 吃亏了 can also mean being taken advantage of.
Disapproving. 爱占小便宜 describes someone always after small gains, like grabbing extra free samples or never paying their share.
The character shows a knife 刃 over a heart 心. Holding back anger is often praised as wisdom: 忍一时风平浪静 ("hold back once and the storm passes").
Frustration that can't be let out, as when someone can't talk back to the boss. 心里憋屈 means feeling wronged and stuck with it.
Humiliated and unable to fight back, as in 受窝囊气. Calling a man 窝囊废 is a harsh insult: spineless.
Usually praise: modesty about wealth or success is admired. 低调奢华 means understated luxury.
Expected when praised: the reply 哪里哪里 ("not at all") is standard, and accepting praise too readily can seem arrogant.

gloss: (of a person or style etc) reserved
note: Usually praise for reserve: feelings are hinted, not declared. A 含蓄 person might never say 我爱你 outright.
Praise for tactful speech. A 委婉 refusal might be 不太方便 ("not very convenient") in place of a plain no.
Often a sigh that someone is easily exploited: 老实人吃亏, "honest people lose out".
A criticism: someone who never offends anyone and never commits to anything. Not the same as tactful.
Mild criticism: a 世故 person knows exactly whom to please. 圆滑世故 ("slick and worldly") is clearly negative.
Praise for someone straightforward and dependable who means what they say and gives a fair price. 人很实在 is a common compliment.
Everyday, informal praise for a person or plan: someone who shows up and does what they promised. 不靠谱 means unreliable or far-fetched.
Very common in speech and online for anything absurd, like a crazy price or a wild rumour: 太离谱了！ "That's ridiculous!"
Slang for a weird person or bizarre behaviour, usually mocking: 奇葩同事 ("weird coworker"). Literally a rare flower, once a compliment.
A common casual put-down for clothes, music or taste that looks rural or old-fashioned: 这衣服太土了.
A compliment on clothes or style, linking stylish with Western. The opposite is 土 ("countrified").
Popular praise for people, ads or officials that connect with ordinary life, such as a leader eating at a street stall.

gloss: to act like a spoiled child; to act coquettishly
note: Pouting and wheedling to get one's way, typical of a child with parents or a girlfriend with a boyfriend. Usually seen as cute rather than annoying.
A common criticism of someone making a fuss over nothing: 别矫情了 ("stop being so dramatic").
Casual and online slang, often about a partner who picks fights or makes demands to test the other. 别作了 means "stop the drama".

gloss: (coll.) presenting as unfriendly and blunt, but warm and tender inside (loanword from Japanese "tsundere")
note: Online and anime slang for a character who acts cold while secretly caring, blushing while saying they don't like someone.
Colloquial and common online: tiredness from dealing with people and situations rather than physical effort, said with a sigh after family drama.
Mostly online and casual, for exasperation at something ridiculous: 我真的无语了.

gloss: to struggle (mentally) with (sth); to overthink; to feel conflicted
note: Very common in everyday talk for being torn over a choice: 我很纠结 ("I can't decide").
Short for 社会性死亡 ("social death"). Common online for public embarrassment, like tripping on stage or posting in the wrong group chat.

gloss: (slang) to break through sb's emotional defenses; to get to sb emotionally
note: Online slang. A touching or upsetting video can make someone say 我破防了 ("that got to me").

gloss: (slang) to compete to an unhealthy degree; hypercompetitive
note: Online and office slang, short for 内卷. 别卷了 ("stop overdoing it") is said to colleagues who stay until midnight.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2014) (slang) to stop striving (esp. when one knows one cannot succeed); to let it all go to hell; (sports) to tank
note: Online slang, often self-mocking. A student who gives up on exams and plays games instead is 摆烂.
Casual praise: 太牛了 ("that's amazing"), or 牛人 for someone impressive. 牛逼 is the vulgar version.
Associated with snow, blunt humour and old heavy industry, much of it hit by the decline of state factories.
Palace insiders who served the emperor up close, often powerful and widely hated. Also used as an insult for a man.
Used for over a thousand years to pick officials. Passing could lift a family from poverty into the ruling class; today's 高考 is often compared to it.

gloss: a person who has passed the county level imperial exam (historical)
note: The first degree in the old exams. Now it suggests a bookish, impractical man: 秀才遇到兵，有理说不清 ("a scholar meeting a soldier can't win by reason").

gloss: yamen, government office in dynastic China
note: Still used sarcastically for bureaucratic offices that are slow or hard to deal with.
A folk ideal of the honest official who stands up to the powerful for ordinary people. Judge Bao, 包青天, is the model.
The hero of 武侠 stories: a wandering swordsman who rights wrongs outside the law. 大侠 is also a joking way to address someone.

gloss: martial arts chivalry (Chinese literary, theatrical and cinema genre)
note: Flying swordsmen, secret techniques and codes of honour. Jin Yong (金庸) is the best-known author of 武侠小说, martial arts novels.
Echoes the outlaw heroes of the Water Margin. 好汉不吃眼前亏 means a sensible man avoids a fight he can't win.
Implies organised, large-scale seizure, as by an army or a colonial power, rather than a single theft.
Strongly negative in schoolbooks and official language, tied to foreign powers carving up China.
A strong word, often used of national humiliation, as in history lessons on past defeats and the 百年屈辱 ("century of humiliation").

gloss: national humiliation, refers to Japanese incursions into China in the 1930s and 40s, and more especially to Mukden railway incident of 18th September 1931 九一八事變|九一八事变 and subsequent Japanese annexation of Manchuria
note: Used in schools and official speeches about Japanese and Western aggression. 勿忘国耻 ("never forget national humiliation") is a common slogan.

gloss: war of resistance, especially the war against Japan (1937-1945)
note: Short for 抗日战争. The subject of family stories, countless films and TV dramas, and official memorial days.

gloss: refers to the Communists' victory over the Nationalists in 1949
note: People date things 解放前 or 解放后, before or after 1949.
Common in official language and the media for China itself, 中国崛起, spoken of with pride after the 百年屈辱 ("century of humiliation").
Online slang: 被和谐了 means a post was deleted or blocked. The joke plays on the official slogan 和谐社会 ("harmonious society").
A top priority in official language: 稳定压倒一切 ("stability overrides everything"). 维稳, "maintaining stability", covers policing unrest.
Official term for the security work that heads off protests and petitions before they start.
Upbeat content of the kind state media promotes. Can be sincere praise or a dig at propaganda.

gloss: (of a movie) created with the purpose of promoting Party values and point of view
note: Literally "main melody". A label for films and shows promoting Party values, usually with patriotic heroes and a predictable ending.
Neutral and everyday: a company can 宣传 a new product, and posters on every street are 宣传. The Party's 宣传部 runs official messaging.
Valued above the individual from school onward. 集体荣誉 ("group honour") is a real motive in class and at work.

gloss: to close a country to exclude foreign contact
note: Usually aimed at the Ming and Qing sea bans, as shorthand for how China fell behind the West. Also used against any inward-looking policy.

gloss: a person with knowledge and experience (idiom)
note: Formal and written, common in appeals and recruitment: 欢迎有识之士加入, "capable people are welcome to join".
A modest answer to how something went, covering anything from fine to bad. It also means careless: 做事马马虎虎.

gloss: lit. draw legs on a snake (idiom); fig. to ruin the effect by adding sth superfluous
note: From a story of a man who finished drawing his snake first, added feet, and lost the prize of wine. A warning against needless additions.
From the farmer who saw a rabbit break its neck on a tree stump, then waited by the stump for another. Used to mock passivity.
From the fable of a shepherd who mended his pen after losing a sheep, to save the rest. Often completed as 亡羊补牢，为时未晚.
From the Han Feizi story of a seller who claimed his spear (矛) could pierce anything and his shield (盾) could stop anything.

gloss: fig. offering a treat to an unappreciative audience
note: Literally "playing the lute to a cow". Said in frustration when an explanation is wasted on someone who can't appreciate it.

gloss: (fig.) a person of limited outlook and experience
note: From the fable of a frog in a well that thinks the sky is as small as the opening. A put-down for someone narrow-minded.
From the old man whose lost horse came back leading another. Often said in full: 塞翁失马，焉知非福 ("who knows it isn't luck?").

gloss: (fig.) to maintain one's resolve for revenge
note: From King Goujian of Yue, who slept on brushwood and tasted gall to remember his defeat. Now also used for any long, patient effort to come back.
From Xiang Yu, who smashed his cooking pots and sank his boats so his army had to win. Used for all-or-nothing commitment.

gloss: fig. to console oneself with illusions
note: From the story of soldiers who stopped feeling thirsty when told of a plum grove ahead. Used for comforting oneself with hopes that won't come true.

gloss: lit. the fox exploits the tiger's might (idiom); fig. to use powerful connections to intimidate people
note: From the fable of a fox walking ahead of a tiger, so the animals fled from the tiger behind it. Used for underlings who throw a boss's weight around.
From the thief who covered his own ears while stealing a bell, thinking no one would hear. Used for obvious self-deception.
From a man who saw a bow's reflection in his wine, thought he had swallowed a snake and fell ill. Used of needless suspicion.

gloss: lit. a notch on the side of a boat to locate a sword dropped overboard (idiom); fig. an action made pointless by changed circumstances
note: From the man who marked his boat where his sword fell overboard, to search there later. Used to mock rigid thinking.

gloss: to spoil things through excessive enthusiasm (idiom)
note: From a farmer who pulled on his seedlings to help them grow, and killed them. Often said of pushing children too fast.

gloss: a crane in a flock of chicken (idiom); way above the common
note: Praise for someone who clearly stands out in a group, often for looks, height or talent.

gloss: to give up halfway (idiom); leave sth unfinished
note: A mild reproach, as when parents scold a child who quits piano after a month: 不要半途而废.

gloss: fig. to be practical and realistic
note: Also a famous Party slogan, so it runs through official speeches about being practical. In daily talk it means being honest about the facts.

gloss: as it should be by rights (idiom); proper and to be expected as a matter of course
note: Often critical: 把别人的帮助当成理所当然, "taking other people's help for granted".

gloss: (idiom) baffling; bizarre; without rhyme or reason; inexplicable
note: Common in everyday complaints: 他莫名其妙地发火了 ("he blew up for no reason"). Alone, 莫名其妙！ means "that makes no sense!"

gloss: May you have a prosperous New Year! (New Year's greeting)
note: The standard Lunar New Year greeting. Children often joke back 红包拿来 ("now hand over the red envelope").

gloss: (idiom) when in Rome, do as the Romans do
note: Said when trying local food or customs on a trip, or to advise a newcomer to fit in.
Literally "seven up, eight down", said of a heart in suspense: 心里七上八下, as when waiting for exam results.
Literally "one hair from nine oxen". For a billionaire, the fine is 九牛一毛.

gloss: to fall in love at first sight (idiom)
note: Common in romance stories and talk about dating. The contrast is 日久生情, love that grows over time.

gloss: shared delights and common hardships (idiom); to share life's joys and sorrows
note: Said of couples, friends or partners who stuck together through hard times, such as years of poverty.

gloss: to have a whole new level of respect for sb or sth
note: Said when someone surprises others by improving, like a struggling student who suddenly aces exams: 让人刮目相看.

gloss: to review the old and know the new (idiom, from the Analects)
note: From Confucius in the Analects, and classic advice to students. Also used for drawing new insight from history.

gloss: with familiarity you learn the trick (idiom); practice makes perfect
note: A standard line from teachers and parents to encourage practice, such as writing characters over and over.
Mostly used in praise of Chinese culture, said with pride: 中华文化博大精深.

gloss: (idiom) of long standing; with a long history; stretching back to ancient times
note: A set phrase in formal writing and speeches, above all about Chinese civilisation's long, continuous history: 中华文化源远流长.
A classical ideal of living in harmony with nature. Mostly found in writing about philosophy and tradition.

gloss: to endure humiliation as part of an important mission (idiom); to suffer in silence
note: A term of praise, often for historical figures who swallowed insults to serve a larger cause.

gloss: to abandon self for others (idiom, from Analects); to sacrifice one's own interest for other people
note: A virtue held up in school lessons and model-hero stories, such as those about 雷锋.
A virtue from revolutionary slogans praising officials who serve the people. Can sound like a slogan.
A Party slogan taught in schools, praising hard work and frugal living as revolutionary virtues.
A Mao-era slogan urging China to depend on no one. Now also said of a person who supports themselves.

gloss: a hundred schools of thought contend (idiom); refers to the classical philosophic schools of the Warring States period 475-221 BC
note: Names the flowering of Confucian, Daoist, Legalist and other ideas before the Qin unified China. Often paired with 百花齐放 in calls for open debate.

gloss: a hundred flowers bloom (idiom); let the arts have free expression
note: Also recalls Mao's 1956 Hundred Flowers campaign, an invitation to free debate that ended in a crackdown on critics. Now used plainly for variety in the arts.

gloss: to keep up with the times
note: An official slogan, so it can sound earnest or bureaucratic.

gloss: making a deer out to be a horse (idiom); deliberate misrepresentation
note: From Zhao Gao, a Qin minister who called a deer a horse to see which officials dared contradict him. Used for twisting facts as a show of power.

gloss: fig. theoretical discussion that is worse than useless in practice
note: From Zhao Kuo, a general who knew the military books by heart but lost his army in battle. Used to dismiss armchair plans.

gloss: fig. to return home after making good
note: Literally "to return home in brocade", now said of anyone who comes back to their hometown having made it, such as arriving in a new car.

gloss: In old age, an expatriate longs to return home.
note: Literally "fallen leaves return to the root". Said of emigrants who want to return, or be buried, in their home village.

gloss: to live in peace and work happily (idiom)
note: The old ideal of a well-governed land, still common in official speeches.

gloss: the country prospers, the people at peace (idiom); peace and prosperity
note: A common wish on New Year couplets and banners, and in official speeches.
Used for duties seen as beyond question: children repaying their parents is 天经地义.
From a scholar named Sun Shan who came last on the pass list; his friend's son ranked below him and failed. A light, literary way to say someone failed.

gloss: to win top marks in the imperial examinations
note: Today a standard good wish to students taking the 高考.

gloss: fig. to study diligently in the face of hardship
note: From a poor boy who drilled a hole in the wall to read by his neighbour's light. Used to praise hard study.
From two scholars, one who tied his hair to a roof beam and one who jabbed his thigh with an awl to stay awake. Held up to students as a model of diligence.

gloss: to start practicing at the first crow of the cock (idiom)
note: From Zu Ti, a general who got up at the first cock crow to drill with his sword. Used to praise hard, early practice.

gloss: lit. every tree or bush an enemy soldier (idiom); fig. to panic and treat everyone as an enemy
note: From Fu Jian at the Battle of Fei River, who took the bushes on a hillside for enemy soldiers. Used of panic and paranoia.

gloss: fig. surrounded by enemies, isolated and without help
note: From Xiang Yu, besieged at Gaixia, hearing the songs of his home state of Chu from the enemy camp.

gloss: fig. to regroup and come back even stronger
note: Used of a rival or team making a comeback, and also of problems returning: 疫情卷土重来.

gloss: lit. fight with one's back to the river (idiom); fig. to fight to win or die
note: From the general Han Xin, who camped his army with a river behind it so they had to win. Used for any all-or-nothing final effort.
Literally to retreat three days' march. Often used for keeping well away from a difficult person, such as a relative at family gatherings.

gloss: lit. to return the jade annulus to Zhao (idiom); fig. to return something intact to its rightful owner
note: Said when returning anything borrowed in good condition. From Lin Xiangru, who brought the He Shi jade safely back to Zhao from Qin.

gloss: fig. to offer sb a humble apology
note: From the general Lian Po, who carried thorns on his back to apologise to the minister Lin Xiangru.

gloss: fig. to make earnest and repeated requests of sb
note: From Liu Bei visiting Zhuge Liang's hut three times to win him over. Used of earnestly recruiting someone talented.

A literary sigh from old stories and poems about beauties who died young or lived unhappily. Sounds fatalistic and old-fashioned today.
Standard for crowds at tourist sites on public holidays, such as West Lake during Golden Week.

gloss: to amaze the world with a single brilliant feat (idiom); an overnight celebrity
note: Part of the saying 不鸣则已，一鸣惊人, from a bird silent for years that then astonished everyone. Used of an unknown who suddenly succeeds.

gloss: not feel ashamed to ask and learn from one's subordinates
note: From the Analects, where Confucius praises a man for not being ashamed to ask those beneath him. Used as praise for humble learning.

gloss: the old man moves mountains (idiom); fig. where there's a will, there's a way

gloss: publicly funded institution, enterprise or foundation
note: As in 事业单位, state-funded institutions such as schools and hospitals. Parents prize jobs there for stability and pensions.
More than a job: 事业有成 means having built something people respect.
A social class as much as a job. Also thrown as an insult for someone unsophisticated, which reflects the rural and urban divide.
Once the honoured class. A factory job meant a secure 铁饭碗, which many lost in the 1990s layoffs.
Marks a decision after weighing things up: 还是走吧 ("we'd better go").
Strong and often annoyed: 我根本不知道 ("I had no idea at all"), pushing back against a suggestion.

gloss: good; correct; conforming to a standard
note: Common praise for pronunciation: 你的普通话很标准 is a real compliment.
Carries history from the 批斗 sessions of the Cultural Revolution. Also used lightly: 思想斗争 means being torn over a decision.
原则上不行 ("not allowed in principle") often leaves room for an exception, if the right person asks.
我对他有意见 means being unhappy with someone, not having thoughts about them.

Common in unfavourable comparisons: 你看看人家 ("look how well others do"), a classic line from parents.

gloss: I, me (referring to oneself as "one" or "people")
note: Coy or sulky, mostly from women or children: 人家不要嘛 ("I don't want to!").
我家姑娘 ("my girl") sounds fonder and more casual than 女儿, the way parents talk to neighbours.
Praise from teachers and bosses. A 积极分子 is an activist on the path to Party membership, so it can tease someone for trying too hard.
Saying a partner is 很物质 means they care about money and what can be bought for them. Rarely a compliment.
注意身体 ("take care of your health") is a common sign-off, especially with elders. 身体好吗 is a caring question.

gloss: a characteristic; a distinctive feature or quality
note: Prominent in official phrases like 中国特色社会主义. Also used half-jokingly for anything that only makes sense in China.
真是个人才 is often a tease, said when someone does something absurdly clever or just absurd.
Formal and written, used in speeches and essays; people call their own mother 妈. It sounds solemn and respectful.

gloss: secretary (chief official of a branch of a socialist or communist party)
note: In a city or university, the Party 书记 outranks the mayor or president and is usually the one who decides.
The classic reply to a compliment, often doubled: 哪里哪里 ("oh, not at all"). Accepting praise outright can sound immodest.
Muttered in annoyance and often left unfinished: 你这人真是… or 真是的！
有手段 describes someone who knows how to get what they want, said with part admiration, part warning.
Said of old-fashioned views on marriage or women: 你太封建了 ("you're so old-fashioned"), half teasing, half serious.

gloss: in those days; back then; in those years
note: 想当年 ("back in my day") is how older people start a story about how things used to be.
这里面有文章 ("there's more to this") means something is going on behind the scenes.

gloss: do not hesitate (to ask, complain etc)
note: A generous offer: 有事尽管说 ("just say if you need anything").
Mostly in 不成气候, said of someone or something that will never amount to much.
Suggests privileged access: 内部价 ("insider price"), 内部消息 ("inside information"). 内部资料 on a document means not for the public.
A generous offer: 有事尽管说 ("just say if you need anything").
Said of old-fashioned views on marriage or women: 你太封建了 ("you're so old-fashioned"), half teasing, half serious.
Common in Taiwan and Hong Kong. On the mainland, people rarely use it for their own home.
Old-fashioned or rural: 她有身子了 ("she's expecting").

gloss: member of a class or group; people of a certain type
note: Often a label for a suspect group: 坏分子, 不法分子 ("lawbreakers"), with a Mao-era ring. 知识分子 ("intellectuals") is neutral.
反映问题 means taking a complaint to someone in charge, a careful, official-sounding way to complain.
Signals disbelief in a rhetorical question: 难道你不知道吗？("Surely you knew?"). The speaker expects the answer to be obvious.
Respectful for someone else's wife, as in 您夫人. For one's own wife it sounds formal or playful.

gloss: to think; to believe (often with the implication that the belief is mistaken – unless referring to one's own current belief)
note: Usually signals the belief was wrong: 我以为他走了 ("I thought he'd left") implies he hadn't.
Also the local neighbourhood office that stamps paperwork and checks on residents. It ran much of daily life during Covid lockdowns.
Among the first things relatives ask children about at New Year.

Until the 1990s the state assigned graduates to jobs, and older people still talk about where their 分配 sent them.

gloss: no thanks (used to politely but informally decline)
note: Lighter than 不要, used to turn down a second helping or an offer: 不了，谢谢.
Real praise, usually meaning good, not merely passable: 这个菜不错 ("this dish is good").
Used for inner conflict: 我很矛盾 ("I'm torn"), wanting two opposite things.
Now slang for classy: 看起来很高级 means it looks expensive and tasteful, and 高级感 is everywhere in fashion and design talk.
Official language: 妇女节, 妇联. Young women may dislike being called 妇女 because it sounds middle-aged.

gloss: (literary) to achieve fame and fortune; to prosper
note: Common in jokes: 等我发达了 ("once I strike it rich"), usually followed by a promise to friends.

gloss: (slang) to fail to catch anything (on a fishing trip); to get skunked
note: Fishing slang: 今天又空军了 ("skunked again today"), said with a laugh among anglers.
Raises the status of the person: 领导亲自来了 sounds like an honour, so 我亲自做的 about one's own cooking is a joke.
Famous from the 1978 slogan 实践是检验真理的唯一标准 ("practice is the sole test of truth"), tied to the start of the reform years.
Formal, mostly in news and writing. 知情人士 ("an informed source") is how reports cite an unnamed insider.
Taught in history class as the force behind China's century of humiliation, so it has a hard, accusatory edge.

Formal, mostly in news and writing. 知情人士 ("an informed source") is how reports cite an unnamed insider.
A mild criticism, often of someone choosing a partner by money or status: 她很现实.
过日子 means everyday living together, and is how couples talk about married life: 好好过日子.
Often means a bad one: 你什么态度？ is a challenge, and 服务态度差 is a common complaint about shops.
Blunt, but friends use it as a plain nickname, and 小胖 is a common name for a chubby kid.
注意形象 ("mind your image") is said to someone being sloppy or loud in public.
School teaches that socialism will replace it. Workers now joke about their bosses as 资本家 ("capitalists").

gloss: to go so far as to
note: 至于吗？is a common retort to someone overreacting: "is that really necessary?"
地下党 brings to mind wartime spy dramas; 地下恋情 is a romance kept hidden.
At work it can be a career word: 要求进步 means wanting promotion or Party membership, in an official tone.
In the Mao years a family's 阶级 label could decide a whole life. Online, 阶级固化 is a complaint that classes no longer move.
As in 红色旅游, tours to old Communist bases like Yan'an, and 红色歌曲, revolutionary songs many older people sing by heart.
Recalls the 路线斗争 ("line struggles") of the Mao era, when being on the wrong line could end a career or worse.
In offices, an instruction from above: 上面下了文件 means it's decided. A 红头文件 ("red-header document") carries official weight.
A 录取通知书 (admission letter) is a family celebration, and relatives call to ask where the student got in.
伸手要钱 means asking for money one hasn't earned, and it makes the person sound shameless.
Two people 配合得好 when they work well together. 请配合 from police or officials is polite but not really a request.
别打击我 ("don't discourage me") is often said half-jokingly to someone who pours cold water on a plan.

gloss: to accept an applicant (prospective student, employee etc) who passes an entrance exam
note: A 录取通知书 (admission letter) is a family celebration, and relatives call to ask where the student got in.
Two people 配合得好 when they work well together. 请配合 from police or officials is polite but not really a request.
别打击我 ("don't discourage me") is often said half-jokingly to someone who pours cold water on a plan.
As a reply, usually lukewarm: 还好吧 means "it's okay", short of praise. A polite way to avoid saying something is good or bad.
An everyday word, not a clinical one: 嗓子发炎 is a sore throat and 伤口发炎 is an infected cut.
Usually disapproving: 安插亲信 means slotting one's own people into posts through connections.
Used for spies and informers placed in secret: 安插眼线 ("plant an informer"), 安插卧底 ("plant a mole").
A standard report workers and students are expected to write: 年终总结 is the year-end review of one's own work, often required by employers.
At work, passing probation to become a regular employee. In the Communist Party, a probationary member becoming a full member.
Usually with 了: 他已经不在了 ("he's no longer with us"). A gentle way to mention a death, common in speech.

gloss: the five social insurances (pension, medical, unemployment, work injury and maternity)
note: Employers are legally required to pay these, usually mentioned as 五险一金 with the housing fund added. Job ads list it as a basic benefit.
Can sound like a challenge: 你是什么人？ demands to know someone's standing. 他是你什么人？ asks how someone is related to the listener.

gloss: to handle; to transact; to conduct
note: The standard verb for paperwork at banks and government offices: 办理手续 ("go through the formalities"), 办理业务.
请你吃饭 means the speaker is paying. Older people still greet with 吃饭了吗？ as a hello rather than a question.
Usually in 靠……吃饭: 靠手艺吃饭 ("live by one's craft"), 靠脸吃饭 ("get by on looks").
Usually 心里嘀咕 or 犯嘀咕: having doubts or misgivings that one keeps to oneself.
At New Year, 回家 usually means travelling back to one's hometown and parents: 回家过年.
The highest level of schooling completed (本科, 硕士), which employers screen on closely. Separate from 学位, the degree actually awarded.
Mostly about manners. 没教养 is a strong insult that reflects on how someone's parents raised them.
The official name in mainland China for standard Mandarin. Taiwan calls it 国语 and Singapore 华语.

gloss: fixed government purchase (esp of farm products)
note: A planned-economy term: the state set quotas of grain, pigs and other farm goods that producers had to sell to it at fixed prices.
Also the usual word for strays: 流浪猫 and 流浪狗 are stray cats and dogs. 流浪汉 is a homeless man.
In entertainment news, a young actress or singer with a pure, innocent image: 玉女明星.
Suggests greedy carving up by stronger parties, as when foreign powers sought to 瓜分中国 in the late Qing. Apps also use it for prize pools: 瓜分百万红包.
看人脸色 means having to watch someone's moods to stay in their favour; 给人脸色看 means showing displeasure through one's expression.

gloss: to compensate for working on a holiday by resting on a workday
note: Part of the official holiday system, where weekends are turned into workdays to make longer breaks. The practice draws frequent complaints.
Often means taking someone's place under false pretences: 冒名顶替. Cases of people taking others' university places this way have caused public outrage.
Ordinary people as opposed to officials. 老百姓 is how people describe themselves in contrast to those in power, and officials use it too.
Also means time: 没功夫 ("no time"), 一会儿功夫 ("a moment"). 下功夫 means putting real effort into something.
Also a polite title for people in the arts, media and other fields who don't teach: 王老师 can be a TV host or an editor.
方便吗？ asks whether now is a good time, for a call or a visit. 不方便 is a polite way to decline without giving a reason.
Mostly comes before something unwelcome: 有点贵 ("a bit pricey"), 有点累 ("a bit tired").
Often means "probably": 应该没问题 ("it should be fine"). 应该的 is a modest reply to thanks: "it was the least I could do".
Also praises things done well: 干得漂亮 ("nicely done"). 说漂亮话 means saying nice-sounding things without meaning them.
After an adjective it means "extremely": 累得不行 ("exhausted"). 他快不行了 can mean he is dying.
An approving word in official histories: 农民起义 ("peasant uprising"). Rebellions seen as illegitimate are called 叛乱 instead.
After the gaokao, 填志愿 means listing one's preferred universities and majors in ranked order; 第一志愿 is the first choice.
公主病 describes a spoiled young woman who expects to be pampered. In KTV venues 公主 is also a euphemism for a hostess.
Often a required registration with the authorities: websites in mainland China must display an ICP 备案 number.
Covers official review of books, films, games and online posts, before or after release. 过审 means passing it.
讨个说法 means pressing those responsible, often officials or a company, to explain and make things right.

gloss: successful candidate in the highest imperial civil service examination
note: The top degree of the imperial examinations, decided by the palace exam in the capital, and the usual route to high office.
Children also call any elderly man 爷爷, and 老爷爷 is a polite way to refer to an old man in general.
Children also call any elderly woman 奶奶, and 老奶奶 is a polite way to refer to an old woman in general.
In Mao-era politics a label of attack, as in 资产阶级思想 ("bourgeois thinking"). 小资, short for 小资产阶级, now means someone with refined middle-class tastes.
In speech it often just means "probably": 估计他不来了, "he's probably not coming".
Long the standard mainland word for husband or wife. Younger speakers more often say 老公 or 老婆, and forms use 配偶.
Someone who acts like a lord expecting to be served. 别把自己当大爷 means "stop acting like you own the place".

gloss: term of respect for older man
note: The usual way to address an old man in the north, stranger or not: 大爷，去车站怎么走？ "Excuse me, sir, how do I get to the station?"

gloss: aunt (affectionate term for an elderly woman)
note: The usual way to address a middle-aged or older woman in the north. In the media, 中国大妈 is a collective label for such women, as shoppers or square dancers.

gloss: to feel jealous (esp. because of a rival in love or affection)
note: Literally "eat vinegar". Often light and teasing, said of partners or of a child jealous of a new sibling.

gloss: to convalesce for a month following childbirth, following a special diet, and observing various taboos to protect the body from exposure to the "wind"
note: Still widely observed: new mothers are often told not to wash their hair, bathe or go outdoors. Paid 月子中心 (postpartum centres) are common in cities.
喝喜酒 means attending a wedding. 什么时候请我们喝喜酒？ is a teasing way of asking someone when they will get married.

gloss: gift money (on the occasion of a wedding etc)
note: Cash given at weddings and similar events, with the amount set by closeness and local custom. Rising amounts are a common complaint.

gloss: money given to children as a gift on Chinese New Year's Eve
note: Given by elders in red envelopes. Parents often take it to keep "for later", a long-running family joke.
Given as gifts to family, colleagues and clients before the festival. Lavish gift boxes have drawn official criticism for extravagance.

gloss: glutinous rice and choice of filling wrapped in leaves and steamed or boiled
note: The food of the Dragon Boat Festival. Whether the filling should be sweet or savoury is a running north-south argument online.
Often based on one's birth date and hour (八字). Some families still consult a fortune-teller about marriage matches or wedding dates.

gloss: year of one's birth sign, according to the cycle of 12 animals of the earthly branches 地支[di4 zhi1]
note: Traditionally an unlucky year, so people wear red underwear, belts or bracelets to ward off bad luck.
Covers scalpers of train tickets, concert tickets and hospital appointment slips. A gang of them is 黄牛党.
Used for cheap clones of brand phones and then for any knockoff or parody. Can be playful as well as dismissive: 山寨版 ("knockoff version").
In revolutionary language, a rural landlord or strongman; the slogan 打土豪，分田地 called for seizing their land.
Someone with lots of money and showy taste. Often joking: 土豪，我们做朋友吧 ("rich guy, let's be friends").

gloss: "Mr Perfect" (i.e. tall, rich and handsome) (Internet slang)
note: An online label for the ideal suitor, often used mockingly, and set against the self-mocking 屌丝 ("loser").

gloss: "Ms Perfect" (i.e. fair-skinned, rich and beautiful) (Internet slang)
note: The female counterpart of 高富帅. 白 is there because pale skin is widely prized as a beauty standard.

gloss: (on social media) to check in to a location
note: Also visiting a trendy place to take photos and post them: 网红打卡地 ("a spot famous online"). Daily habit check-ins are called 打卡 too.
网红店 and 网红餐厅 are places made popular online, often with long queues. The label can suggest style over substance.

gloss: (neologism) (slang) to spark interest in a product or idea (esp. on social media)
note: Shopping slang from social media: 被种草 means being made to want something, and 拔草 means buying it or losing interest.

gloss: (neologism c. 2016) (slang) to watch an entertaining spectacle from the sidelines and-or engage in gossip about it
note: From 吃瓜群众 ("melon-eating masses"), bystanders following celebrity scandals online. Said of oneself, it signals curiosity without taking sides.
An online insult for someone who argues with everything for its own sake, from 抬杠 ("to bicker").
Northeastern slang spread by livestreaming apps, where hosts call viewers 老铁. 老铁，没毛病 means "bro, no problem".
Literally "little fresh meat": a young, good-looking male star. Can be admiring or a jab at young actors seen as all looks and no skill.

gloss: children of entrepreneurs who became wealthy under Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms in the 1980s
note: Now used of any rich family's children, usually with an image of entitlement and showy spending.
Common in stories about privilege. The 我爸是李刚 ("my dad is Li Gang") case made it a byword for using a parent's power to escape consequences.

gloss: (slang) to rely on one's father's wealth or prestige to get ahead
note: Said resentfully of competition decided by family background, not effort: 这年头还得拼爹 ("these days it comes down to who your dad is").

gloss: (coll.) to live with and depend on one's parents even upon reaching adulthood
note: Literally "gnaw on the old", and disapproving. 啃老族 is the label for adults who live off their parents.

gloss: no-frills civil wedding ceremony lacking a material foundation: no car, house, reception, rings, or honeymoon
note: Marrying without the flat, car and big wedding that families often expect. Can be a stand against those expectations or simply what a couple can afford.
A common self-description among urban homeowners paying decades-long mortgages. Owning a flat is widely seen as a precondition for marriage.

gloss: a residential property located within the designated catchment area of a desirable school, often sought after by parents to secure school admission for their children
note: These flats can cost far more than homes nearby, since public school places depend on where a family owns its home.
Mostly ordered through apps such as Meituan; 点外卖 ("order delivery") is an everyday habit, and couriers are called 外卖小哥.

gloss: Moments (social networking function of smartphone app WeChat 微信[Wei1 xin4])
note: The main place people post personal updates: 发朋友圈 ("post on Moments"). Hiding posts from parents or bosses is common.

gloss: (coll.) to scam sb by setting up an "accident" in which one appears to have sustained damage or injury caused by the scam victim, then demanding compensation (variations include putting "expensive" porcelain in a place where it is likely to be knocked over by passers-by, and stepping into the path of a slow-moving car)
note: Also used figuratively for riding on someone else's fame or picking a fight for attention: 碰瓷名人 ("leech off celebrities").
Officers who clear unlicensed street vendors and enforce city rules. Clashes with vendors have given them a rough public image.

gloss: to seek an audience with higher-ups (esp. government officials) to petition for sth
note: Citizens take grievances to higher levels of government through the 信访 ("letters and visits") system, often travelling to provincial capitals or Beijing.

gloss: to demolish a building and relocate the inhabitants
note: Widespread during urban redevelopment. Compensation can make families rich, hence 拆二代, but forced evictions are a common source of disputes.

gloss: householder who refuses to vacate his home despite pressure from property developers
note: Literally "nail household", one that can't be pulled out. Also used of any holdout who refuses to budge.
Blunt and disapproving, aimed at the woman blamed for breaking up a marriage. 打小三 means confronting her, often in public.
A kept mistress supported with money or a flat, an arrangement long associated with wealthy businessmen and officials.

gloss: (coll.) naive or easily exploited people (esp. small investors or consumers), likened to chives that can be repeatedly harvested for profit
note: Investors' slang: 割韭菜 ("harvest the chives") is fleecing small investors again and again, and losers call themselves 韭菜.

gloss: (slang) (neologism derived from 背黑鍋|背黑锅[bei1 hei1 guo1]) to carry the can; to be a scapegoat
note: Office and online slang for taking the blame for someone else's mistake; 背锅侠 is the person who always ends up blamed.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2017) to shift the blame; to pass the buck
note: Common in office talk and political commentary. The opposite of 背锅, and the two often appear together.
Now often a trick or manipulative script: 别跟我玩套路 ("don't play games with me"), 套路太深 ("too many tricks").
Mostly disapproving in modern use: 有心机 or 心机女 describes someone calculating and manipulative.
Common slang for doing something with real care: 这礼物很走心 ("a thoughtful gift"). 不走心 means half-hearted.

gloss: it's none of my business ("I’m just here to buy some soy sauce")
note: A catchphrase for being a mere bystander or having a minor role: 我是来打酱油的 ("I'm just passing through").
Online slang for something so bizarre or tasteless it stuns, like being struck by lightning: 雷人的造型 ("an outrageous outfit").

gloss: (vulgar) (of sth that makes one feel misled or let down etc) to be a big disappointment
note: An online exclamation for a letdown or rip-off: 这电影太坑爹了 ("this film is such a letdown"). Crude-sounding but widely used.

gloss: (coll.) cute; adorable (orthographic borrowing from Japanese 萌え "moe", affection for an anime or manga character)
note: Online it covers anything cute, including adults acting cute (卖萌). 萌萌哒 is a gushing way of saying adorable.

gloss: a guy who stays at home all the time, typically spending a lot of time playing online games (derived from Japanese "otaku")
note: Can be self-mocking or dismissive. It usually means an introverted homebody, not specifically an anime fan.

gloss: fan; enthusiast for sb or sth (loanword from "fans")
note: Also the follower count on social media: 粉丝多 ("lots of followers"). A star's fans often go by a collective nickname.
Organised celebrity fandom that buys in bulk, boosts rankings and attacks critics online. Authorities have cracked down on its excesses.

gloss: (neologism c. 2017) (slang) young lady (amiable form of address for a young woman of about one's own age or a little older)
note: A friendly, slightly cute word for a young woman, common online and with strangers. Often preferred to 小姐, which can suggest a sex worker.

gloss: square dancing, an exercise routine performed to music in public squares, parks and plazas, popular esp. among middle-aged and retired women in China
note: Loud music from groups of dancers is a common neighbourhood complaint, and disputes over noise and space make regular news.
Used in exasperation, often online about children who damage things in public, with the parents blamed as 熊家长.
Also 妈宝男. A sharp criticism in dating talk of a man who defers to his mother in everything, including his marriage.

gloss: (Internet slang) guy who grew up in the countryside and gained a foothold in the city through hard work
note: Often critical in marriage talk, implying he puts his rural family's demands before his urban wife. Contrasted with 孔雀女, a city-raised woman.

gloss: (coll.) "leftover man" – a man who remains single beyond the typical marrying age
note: Less of an insult than 剩女. It often points to rural men unable to find wives because of the gender imbalance.
Couples who choose this often face pressure from parents. The word is used as a self-label and in debates about falling birth rates.
The generation born under the one-child policy, in force from about 1980 to 2015. Media often stereotype them as spoiled 小皇帝 ("little emperors").
The official name for state birth limits, chiefly the one-child policy, run by local family planning offices. Not a private choice about contraception.

gloss: "left-behind children", rural children whose parents have to make a living as migrant workers in distant urban areas, but cannot afford to keep the family with them
note: Usually raised by grandparents in the home village. A recognised social problem, regularly covered in news and government policy.
Mostly heard in 空巢老人, elderly people living alone because their children work elsewhere, a common topic in news on ageing.
Best known from 小康社会 ("moderately prosperous society"), the long-running official development goal, declared achieved in 2021.
Mostly done at Spring Festival, when families go round relatives' homes in turn, bringing gifts.

gloss: to pay a New Year call
note: Done in person, by phone or by message during Spring Festival. Children who 拜年 to elders expect a 红包 in return.

gloss: to stay up all night on lunar New Year's Eve
note: A family custom of staying up past midnight together on New Year's Eve, now often in front of the 春晚 TV gala.

gloss: reunion dinner on Lunar New Year's Eve (Chinese New Year tradition)
note: The most important family meal of the year; people travel across the country to be home for it. Fish is served for 年年有余 ("surplus every year").
Set off at New Year, weddings and shop openings to scare off bad luck and make noise. Many cities now ban them.

gloss: Spring Festival couplet (the first line of which is pasted on the right side of a doorway at New Year, and the second on the left side)
note: Written on red paper with lucky wishes and topped by a horizontal 横批 over the door. Put up in the days before New Year.
Traditionally needed for any proper marriage. Today often a relative or neighbour who sets up a 相亲 (arranged blind date).

gloss: to go and live with one's wife's family, in effect becoming a member of her family
note: Traditionally a loss of face for the man, and the children may take the wife's surname. The colloquial word is 倒插门.

gloss: (of the husband) to marry into and live with the wife's family (inverting traditional Chinese expectations)
note: Colloquial and often mocking; the formal word is 入赘. A man who marries in this way still faces some stigma in many places.
Casual and a little jokey, used by men about their wife's father, not to his face. Formal is 岳父.

gloss: adoptive father (traditional adoption, i.e. without legal ramifications)
note: Often a family friend formally taken as a child's godfather. Online it is also slang for a sugar daddy.

gloss: (dialect) close childhood friend whom one grew up with
note: Originally Beijing speech, now widespread: a friend since early childhood, usually from the same street or compound. Closer than 老同学.
Northern and affectionate, used by parents about their own daughter: 我闺女今年上大学 ("my girl starts university this year").
A lifestyle drawn from traditional medicine: herbal teas, eating by season, early nights. 朋克养生 mocks young people doing it half-heartedly.
Things like ginseng, bird's nest and 阿胶, believed in traditional medicine to build strength. Common gifts for elders and new mothers.
Self-applied and fond: 我是个吃货 means "I love my food", with no shame attached. The insult sense is now rare.
A familiar scandal topic in hospitals and public procurement, such as doctors taking 回扣 from drug companies.
Includes gifts to officials, teachers or bosses to get things done, which many see as a social burden. Also covers ordinary gifts when visiting.
Colloquial and contemptuous, usually about flattering bosses. A habitual flatterer is a 马屁精.

gloss: to have one's life made difficult by sb (usu. by sb in a position of authority) (lit. to be made to wear tight shoes)
note: Office politics: 给他穿小鞋 means a superior getting back at someone with petty obstacles and unfair tasks.
A criticism of officials or clerks who answer with rules and stock phrases instead of actually helping.
Common in complaints about officials and companies: giving vague answers and pushing the matter elsewhere.

gloss: (fig.) actions that are technically legal but perhaps not respectable
note: Online, 擦边 often means racy content that stays just inside the rules, such as 擦边视频 on video apps.
A standard complaint about offices that send people back and forth between departments, each saying it is not their job.

gloss: to be made a scapegoat; to be unjustly blamed
note: Online often shortened to 背锅; 甩锅 means pushing blame onto someone else.
Often said of inspections, meetings and campaigns held only for show.

gloss: lit. to cut all at one stroke (idiom); to impose uniformity
note: Almost always a criticism of rules applied rigidly to everyone regardless of local conditions, such as blanket bans.

gloss: excessive concern with form over substance
note: A stock criticism in official Party language, often paired with 官僚主义. Also used of pointless paperwork and meetings at work.
As a description it is a criticism: 太官僚了 means high-handed and unhelpful, not just procedural.
Said of people who act superior and keep others at a distance. 没架子 ("no airs") is praise for an approachable boss or official.

gloss: to do a secret or dishonest deal
note: Using connections or position to get jobs, school places or permits around the rules. 走后门 is the side receiving the favour.

gloss: unspoken rules (usually ones that codify improper behaviors such as leveraging guanxi to get favorable treatment, or coercing employees for sexual favors)
note: Also a verb: 被潜规则 means being pressured into sex in exchange for a role or promotion, especially in show business.
Jokingly, a spouse's secret savings: 老公的小金库 ("hubby's secret stash").
In official language, off-the-books funds kept by a work unit, a regular target of audits and discipline campaigns.
Strongly tied to the campaign begun in 2012, with slogans like 打老虎、拍苍蝇 ("hit tigers and swat flies"), meaning senior and junior officials alike.

gloss: shuanggui, an extralegal system within the CCP for detaining and interrogating cadres who fall from grace
note: Short for requiring a cadre to answer at a set time and place (规定时间、规定地点). Replaced in 2018 by 留置 under the new supervision system.

gloss: to demote a party cadre to work on the shop floor or in the countryside
note: Best known from the Mao era, when cadres and intellectuals were sent to the countryside or factories for labour and reform.

gloss: to redress (an injustice); to rehabilitate (sb whose reputation was unjustly sullied)
note: Used above all for the late 1970s and 1980s, when many people labelled rightists or counterrevolutionaries were officially cleared.
In PRC history, the label given to people targeted in the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign. It barred them from normal careers for about two decades.

gloss: model theater (operas and ballets produced during the Cultural Revolution)
note: For years almost the only stage works allowed, beginning with eight approved pieces such as 红灯记. Older people still know the arias.

gloss: coupons for food or grain used in a PRC economic program c. 1955-1993
note: Needed alongside cash to buy grain under rationing. Now a symbol of the planned-economy years and a collector's item.

gloss: household with savings or annual income of 10,000 yuan or more (considered a large amount in the 1970s, when the term became established)
note: A byword for early reform-era wealth. Now used nostalgically or jokingly, given how little 10,000 yuan buys today.
Small family businesses such as stalls, shops and repair stands, which grew in the early reform years and were once looked down on next to state jobs.
Associated with the 1980s, when traders bought scarce goods at low state prices and resold them on the market. Mildly disparaging.

gloss: migrant worker living and working in Beijing or Taipei without a residence permit
note: Mainly about Beijing: young people without a Beijing 户口 who rent cheap rooms to chase work there. Often used of themselves.

gloss: to live (in a tiny, cramped space)
note: Self-mocking word for cramped city housing, made popular by a 2009 TV series of that name about housing prices.
Old villages surrounded by expanding cities, packed with cheap rentals for migrant workers. Many have been demolished for redevelopment.

gloss: a property providing rural accommodation (farm stay, boutique hotel etc)
note: A weekend outing for city people: farm meals, fishing and mahjong at a rural guesthouse near town.

gloss: to go to a local market or country fair (on market day)
note: Rural markets are held on fixed days, often set by the lunar calendar; 赶 conveys hurrying to get there.
Mostly held at Spring Festival, with snacks, folk shows and stalls; in Beijing at parks such as 地坛.

gloss: (used to describe sb or sth that makes a very strong impression, whether favorable or unfavorable) terrible; intense; severe; devastating; amazing; awesome; outstanding
note: Mostly praise in everyday talk: 你真厉害！ ("you're amazing"). Of pain or illness it means severe: 疼得厉害 ("it hurts badly").

gloss: (fig.) to make an extra effort; to cheer sb on
note: The all-purpose cheer, shouted at races and typed before exams or interviews: 加油！ ("come on!", "you can do it").
Often looser than it sounds: a courier's 马上到 ("almost there") can mean several more minutes.
The everyday word husbands use for their wife, casual and affectionate. 妻子 is the written form, and 爱人 sounds older.
Polite and a little old-fashioned on the mainland, more common in Hong Kong and Taiwan: 王太太 ("Mrs Wang"). 阔太太 is a rich man's wife.
Livestreamed selling is big business: 直播带货 means a host selling products live, and the host is a 主播.
Often means a romantic relationship: 感情问题 ("relationship problems"), 他们感情很好 ("they're very close").
An everyday word, not a clinical one: 嗓子发炎 is a sore throat and 伤口发炎 is an infected cut.
A standard report workers and students are expected to write: 年终总结 is the year-end review of one's own work, often required by employers.
Usually with 了: 他已经不在了 ("he's no longer with us"). A gentle way to mention a death, common in speech.
请你吃饭 means the speaker is paying. Older people still greet with 吃饭了吗？ as a hello rather than a question.
The highest level of schooling completed (本科, 硕士), which employers screen on closely. Separate from 学位, the degree actually awarded.
Also the usual word for strays: 流浪猫 and 流浪狗 are stray cats and dogs. 流浪汉 is a homeless man.
Suggests greedy carving up by stronger parties, as when foreign powers sought to 瓜分中国 in the late Qing. Apps also use it for prize pools: 瓜分百万红包.

gloss: to compensate for resting on a workday by working on a holiday
note: Part of the official holiday system, where weekends are turned into workdays to make longer breaks. The practice draws frequent complaints.
Also means time: 没功夫 ("no time"), 一会儿功夫 ("a moment"). 下功夫 means putting real effort into something.
An approving word in official histories: 农民起义 ("peasant uprising"). Rebellions seen as illegitimate are called 叛乱 instead.

Often a required registration with the authorities: websites in mainland China must display an ICP 备案 number.
Covers official review of books, films, games and online posts, before or after release. 过审 means passing it.
The top degree of the imperial examinations, decided by the palace exam in the capital, and the usual route to high office.
In Mao-era politics a label of attack, as in 资产阶级思想 ("bourgeois thinking"). 小资, short for 小资产阶级, now means someone with refined middle-class tastes.
Someone who acts like a lord expecting to be served. 别把自己当大爷 means "stop acting like you own the place".
Used for cheap clones of brand phones and then for any knockoff or parody. Can be playful as well as dismissive: 山寨版 ("knockoff version").

In revolutionary language, a rural landlord or strongman; the slogan 打土豪，分田地 called for seizing their land.
Often based on one's birth date and hour (八字). Some families still consult a fortune-teller about marriage matches or wedding dates.
Online slang for something so bizarre or tasteless it stuns, like being struck by lightning: 雷人的造型 ("an outrageous outfit").
Common slang for doing something with real care: 这礼物很走心 ("a thoughtful gift"). 不走心 means half-hearted.
Blunt and disapproving, aimed at the woman blamed for breaking up a marriage. 打小三 means confronting her, often in public.
A kept mistress supported with money or a flat, an arrangement long associated with wealthy businessmen and officials.

Organised celebrity fandom that buys in bulk, boosts rankings and attacks critics online. Authorities have cracked down on its excesses.

gloss: a home where the kids have grown up and moved out
note: Mostly heard in 空巢老人, elderly people living alone because their children work elsewhere, a common topic in news on ageing.
Best known from 小康社会 ("moderately prosperous society"), the long-running official development goal, declared achieved in 2021.

gloss: to wish sb a Happy New Year
note: Done in person, by phone or by message during Spring Festival. Children who 拜年 to elders expect a 红包 in return.

gloss: to see in the New Year
note: A family custom of staying up past midnight together on New Year's Eve, now often in front of the 春晚 TV gala.

Class background as assigned under Mao: a 地主 (landlord) or 贫农 (poor peasant) label shaped schooling, jobs and safety. 成分不好 meant a bad class label.

gloss: huge; great; grand; worthy of the greatest admiration; important (contribution etc)
note: Heavily official in tone: 伟大的祖国, 伟大领袖. Not used for everyday praise, where 太好了 or 了不起 fit better.
